newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher, except palladium.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher, except palladium.

text.p: New York precious metals recovered from some early weakness to end higher Thursday, with the exception of palladium which gave back Wednesday's gains after news Russia may resume exports to Japan in May.
"There's some interest in the platinum metals group but it's not doing much for gold or silver yet," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said.

"Open interest has fallen away in COMEX gold and the funds look to be more interested now in the grains and softs like coffee, so it's hard to know what's going to break gold out of it's recent range."
COMEX June gold ended up 50 cents at $351.00 an ounce, with support still seen around $350 and resistance around $352.00, within the $348.30-358.00 range of the past month.
In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $348.40/90, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $347.60 and the New York close Wednesday around $347.80/30.

Gold has traded in increasingly narrower ranges in recent weeks, and COMEX gold open interest has declined to its lowest level in over a year, with 20 day historical volatility falling back to around nine percent Thursday from 16 percent in mid-March.
The bias is still probably to the downside, analysts said, with potential central bank and producer sales capping the market, and longer term moving-averages suggesting gold is still in a downtrend.
But physical demand was good at prices below $350 early this year, and low short term implied lease rates suggest there is little interest in shorting the market further, analysts said.

The Philadelphia Stocks Exchange's gold and silver sector index of North American mining stock prices (.XAU) was up a solid 2.98 points at 104.04 near the close, and may be finally found some support again after reaching oversold levels last week in the wake of the collapse in the price of Canadian mining junior Bre-X in recent weeks.
COMEX May silver ended up 0.7 cent at $4.780 an ounce, but the contract is still struggling to recover from a contract low at $4.655 seen last Thursday.
Traders said there was little chance Friday's expiry of COMEX and NYMEX metal options would give May silver a boost as open interest was heaviest at prices above $5.00, well above the current market.
On the other hand, silver's downside below $5.00 was probably limited, traders said, as the fundamentals are much better than in February 1993 when silver made a 19-year low at $3.50.
Reported inventories are only half the February 1993 levels and sizable deficits between mine supply and fabrication demand are seen persisting.
NYMEX July platinum ended up 80 cents at $373.90 an ounce, while the October NYMEX platinum/COMEX gold spread widened further to $20.70 an ounce, from around $19.30 Wednesday.
NYMEX June palladium recovered from a morning low at $153.70, but still closed off $4.10 at $155.50.

Spot palladium fixed in London Thursday morning at a new 21 month high at $160.25, after catching up with gains on NYMEX Thursday and on TOCOM overnight, but was quoted in late New York trade around $156.50.
The NYMEX June/September palladium spread went into a rare backwardation Wednesday around $1.50 an ounce, but the spread slipped back to zero Thursday.

In news overnight, the head of the precious metals division in the Russian finance ministry, Victor Rybkin, said a decree may be issued next week providing authority for the resumption of platinum group metals to Japan in May.

But analysts now believe Russia may be in no hurry to resume exports as a new administration is now in place, the IMF has agreed to resume lending to Russia, western capital investment is again flowing into the country, and Russia's fiscal problems may have eased a little.

Further, with auto industry demand for palladium rising quickly, and the U.S. now probably a larger consumer of the metal than Japan, the Russians may now see little advantage in renewing the annual supply contract with the Japanese, prefering to sell at spot market prices, analysts said.
Russian palladium exports have been disrupted since December 1997 after annual supply contract talks with Japan broke down due to fiscal and administrative problems in Russia.
